title: India bars stem cell therapy for autism as routine care
excerpt: The health ministry's September 16 advisory says any stem cell use for autism must remain confined to duly approved clinical trials, following a January 2026 Supreme Court order; unauthorized treatment can now mean professional misconduct charges.
body:
• In a September 16 advisory, the health ministry said stem cell therapy for autism spectrum disorder may be used only in duly approved clinical trials — not as routine or commercial care.
  • The order follows a January 30, 2026 Supreme Court judgment directing the government to regulate stem cell treatments; the NMC says unauthorized use will count as professional misconduct.
  • State medical councils must investigate complaints; violations can trigger registration cancellation and penalties under the Clinical Establishments Act.
  • Families currently paying clinics for such treatments will need to stop commercial therapy, with the court directing a transition plan for patients already undergoing it.

NEW DELHI — India's health ministry has barred stem cell therapy for autism as routine medical care, telling states and Union Territories that any use of stem cells for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) must remain restricted to duly approved clinical trials.

In an advisory dated September 16 and addressed to all states and UTs that have adopted the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, the ministry said the “therapeutic use of any type of stem cell in autism is to remain restricted to duly approved clinical trials, in accordance with the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017, issued jointly by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) and the Department of Biotechnology (DBT).”

The directive is aimed squarely at clinics marketing unproven treatments to desperate families. It seeks, in the ministry's framing, to prevent providers from selling unproven interventions as standard treatment — and warns that non-compliance will bring consequences.

The Supreme Court order behind it

The advisory follows a Supreme Court judgment dated January 30, 2026, in Yash Charitable Trust & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors., which directed the government to regulate stem cell treatments. The court held that non-compliance with the statutory framework must attract consequences — including professional misconduct under Regulation 7.22 of the IMC Regulations, 2002, and action under Sections 32 and 40 of the Clinical Establishments Act, which provide for cancellation of registration and financial penalties, according to Mint's reporting.

On September 5, the National Medical Commission issued its own advisory stating that stem cell therapy can be offered as routine care only for approved indications, and that “unauthorized administration, prescription, promotion or advertisement of stem cell therapy beyond the approved indications would constitute professional misconduct.” State medical councils have been directed to investigate complaints and take disciplinary action.

“Using them as unproven treatments carries not only the risk of failure, but also unexpected adverse health outcomes.”

— Dr Rajeev Jayadevan, public health expert and former IMA president, Kochi chapter

What “bars as routine care” actually means

The bar is on commercial, off-label use — not on research. Stem cell therapy for autism remains legal inside duly approved clinical trials conducted under the NGSCR 2017 framework. It cannot, however, be sold by clinics as standard care, advertised, or prescribed as an established treatment. For autism, the evidence bar has not been met: as Dr Rajeev Jayadevan told Mint, “Stem cells represent a complex and continuously evolving field in healthcare… The reality is far more nuanced” than the belief that these cells can cure common conditions.

What it means for parents

For families who have paid — often heavily — for stem cell interventions for their children, the order is disruptive. The Supreme Court has clarified that therapy already underway cannot continue as a commercial undertaking, but it also directed the ministry, in consultation with AIIMS and the NMC, to provide a solution so such patients can keep receiving therapy until they can be re-routed to institutions conducting clinical trials. Four weeks were given for that transition plan.

States and UTs have been asked to circulate the Supreme Court's directions widely — to state and district regulatory authorities as well as government and private clinical establishments involved in stem cell research, treatment, promotion, or administration — so that the rules reach the clinics actually offering the treatments.

What's next

The immediate test is enforcement: whether state medical councils act on complaints against clinics advertising stem cell “cures” for autism, and how quickly the AIIMS-led transition plan reaches patients mid-treatment. The broader signal is that India's stem cell regime is hardening — as Mint reported on August 19, the government has been issuing strict norms for stem cell therapies — and unproven commercial interventions are increasingly being treated as misconduct, not medicine.
